headline: High-risk defaults: shared filesystem and broad write/network access create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways between Flowise and ms-swift.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write server filesystem and ingest uploaded files; ms-swift can read/write filesystem and emits CLI/Python outputs. A shared workspace or file handoff lets attacker-controlled content from one agent be treated as instructions by the other. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so this is inferred from file-based interaction rather than directly observed.
conditions: IF Flowise writes a file that ms-swift later parses as prompts or config, injection is possible.
IF ms-swift writes logs or outputs into a shared directory that Flowise ingests, injection is possible.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories with OS permissions.
Disable automatic ingestion of shared files in Flowise flows.
Require explicit allowlists for any file parsed as instructions.
Add a manual review step before ms-swift outputs are reused.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent file handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files and secrets, and Flowise has broad network egress while ms-swift calls external model APIs. If they share a workspace or credentials store, sensitive chatflow inputs, model keys, datasets, or checkpoints can flow from one agent into the other's outputs or outbound requests. The pairwise leakage path is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same workspace, leakage risk is present.
IF either agent is configured with shared secret files, those secrets can be exposed in outputs or API calls.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces and secret stores.
Rotate any shared credentials before pairing.
Restrict outbound domains for both agents.
Redact sensitive fields before passing artifacts between agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Flowise can write the server filesystem and supports multiple instances via shared server datastore; ms-swift can execute shell commands, install packages, spawn subprocesses, and write files. In a shared directory or datastore, concurrent writes and environment changes can collide, and ms-swift's stronger local execution makes conflicts more dangerous. No locking mechanism is documented, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents target the same filesystem path, write conflicts can occur.
IF Flowise instances share datastore state while ms-swift mutates adjacent files, race conditions can corrupt artifacts.
mitigations: Assign disjoint filesystem roots to each agent.
Run only one writer per shared directory at a time.
Snapshot shared artifacts before ms-swift modifies them.
Disable package installation in ms-swift for shared environments.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise produces graph-based tool outputs that ms-swift could consume as prompts, configs, or evaluation inputs. ms-swift can then execute shell commands or install packages based on those inputs, so an error or hallucination in Flowise can cascade into concrete actions. Because verification steps are not documented, the safer higher severity is warranted.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes Flowise output without validation, cascading errors can trigger downstream actions.
IF Flowise-generated configuration is used to launch ms-swift jobs, incorrect parameters can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a human approval step before ms-swift acts on Flowise output.
Validate Flowise outputs against a schema before reuse.
Limit ms-swift to read-only dry-run mode for shared inputs.
Log and diff all generated configs before execution.
requires-engineering: add automated verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and tool credentials, while ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data. If regulated or sensitive data is routed through both, differing retention and residency controls can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not state HIPAA/GDPR status, so this is a policy-gap risk rather than a proven violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed in both agents, retention and residency policies must match.
IF one agent logs artifacts that the other retains longer, compliance drift occurs.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it through either agent.
Set matching retention windows for logs and artifacts.
Block regulated data from non-approved flows.
Review vendor residency and DPA terms before deployment.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based retention enforcement.
